paragraphs.heading: A scale built on scratching
paragraphs.text: The Mohs scale rates how well minerals resist being scratched. It runs from 1 to 10 and rests on one idea: a harder material can scratch a softer one. In practice it is based on whether one natural sample of a mineral can visibly scratch another mineral. The German geologist and mineralogist Friedrich Mohs introduced the scale in 1812.

paragraphs.heading: An old idea with a diamond on top
paragraphs.text: Comparing hardness by seeing which minerals can scratch others is a method of great antiquity. Theophrastus mentioned it in his treatise On Stones, around 300 BC, and Pliny the Elder followed in his Naturalis Historia. When the scale was designed, diamond was the hardest naturally occurring mineral known. Diamond defines the top of the scale, which was set, arbitrarily, at 10.

paragraphs.heading: How a hardness is found
paragraphs.text: A reference mineral stands for each of the ten hardness values, and most of these minerals are widespread in rocks. To measure a material against the scale, you find the hardest material it can scratch, or the softest material that can scratch it. Suppose apatite scratches a sample but fluorite does not. The sample's Mohs hardness then lies between 4 and 5.

paragraphs.heading: What counts as a scratch
paragraphs.text: For this scale, scratching has a technical meaning: creating non-elastic dislocations that the naked eye can see. Materials lower on the scale can frequently make microscopic non-elastic dislocations in materials with a higher Mohs number. These microscopic marks are permanent, and they sometimes harm the structural integrity of the harder material. Even so, they are not counted as scratches when a Mohs number is determined.

paragraphs.heading: Steps of unequal size
paragraphs.text: The Mohs scale is a qualitative, ordinal scale. In absolute hardness, corundum, at 9, is twice as hard as topaz, at 8, but diamond, at 10, is about four times as hard as corundum. The Mohs scale is one of several definitions of hardness used in materials science, and some of the others are more quantitative.

paragraphs.heading: Trouble with mixtures
paragraphs.text: Some solid substances that are not minerals have also been given a hardness on the Mohs scale. But hardness can be difficult to determine, or misleading or meaningless, when a material is a mixture of several substances. Granite is an example. Some sources assign it a Mohs hardness between 6 and 7, yet granite is a rock, and each of the several minerals in it has a Mohs hardness of its own. Topaz-rich granite is mainly topaz at 8, quartz at 7, orthoclase at 6, plagioclase at 6–6.5 and mica at 2–4.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is used
paragraphs.text: The Mohs scale lacks precision, but it is relevant for field geologists, who use scratch kits to roughly identify minerals. It does not accurately predict how well materials will endure in industry. It is useful in milling, where it helps assess which kind of mill and grinding medium will best reduce a product whose hardness is known. Electronics manufacturers use the scale to test the resilience of flat panel display components and to evaluate the hardness of touch screens.
